Header: Meloidogyne spp. Root-knot nematode in English, Amashanya in Kinyarwanda language

Prevention: Root-knot nematodes live in the soil in or on roots.
Don’t select a seedbed location from an area previously infected by nematodes, because they stay for long in the soil
Transplant only seedlings with healthy roots, free of nematodes
Use organic soil amendments that increase soil microbial activity and enhance parasites and predators of nematodes, for example.
Apply organic matter from nematode- antagonistic plants such as
Tagetes patula on fields for two months after harvest, plough into soil before planting seedlings.
Apply up to 10 kg per acre or 10-15 tons per ha of manure or compost 10.
Include chicken manure, it releases gases toxic to nematodes
Control volunteer crops or other solanaceous plants
Rotate with crops, that are resistant to those root-knot nematodes. such as sorghum, millet, broccoli, cauliflower, cabbage
Monitoring: Damage is most serious on light sandy soils in furrow-irrigated fields.
Search for plants that are weak & small.
The infected plants may entirely wilt during warm weather and recover at rainy weather.
Uproot an affected plant to check for swellings (knots, galls) on roots.
In case that about 1 out of 4 to 6 plants are infected in the field, consider direct control measures.
Often, the economic threshold is 1-10 root-knot nematodes/200 g soil, but this can only be measured by experts.
In conditions of hot climates and sandy soils, the threshold gets far lower than 10.
Action will be far too late, if most plants are infected
Direct Control: Nematode are easier to prevent than to control.
